big_idea: Two expressions can be EQUAL (same amount) or NOT EQUAL.
learning_intention: We are learning to determine whether given pairs of addition and subtraction expressions are equivalent or not.
student_learning_goal: I can decide if two addition or subtraction expressions are equal.
success_criteria: I can use a balance scale to test if two expressions are equal.
I can use the equal sign (=) when amounts are the same.
I can use the NOT equal sign (≠) when amounts are different.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Bella the Balance Beam Scientist — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

OPTIONAL: Bobby the Balance Beam Buddy — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Real balance scale (or cardboard prop with movable arm)
Lesson 2 equivalence tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Bella has 5+3 on one side. Bobby has 4+4 on the other. Will the balance be level or tipped?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Bella + Bobby puppets. 'Friends — Bella and Bobby have a real balance scale. They want to know — are 5+3 and 4+4 the SAME?'

Place 5 counters on the left pan, 3 more (total 8). On the right pan, place 4 counters, then 4 more (total 8). Show the balance — LEVEL.

'Bella says — when both sides have the SAME amount, the balance is LEVEL. 5+3 and 4+4 BOTH equal 8. They're EQUAL.' Write 5 + 3 = 4 + 4 on the chart with the equal sign highlighted.

Now not-equal. 'Bella has 5+3 on the left. Bobby puts 9 on the right. Same?' Place 8 vs 9. Balance TIPS to the right.

'Tipped! 5+3 is 8, but 9 is more. They're NOT EQUAL. We write that with a special sign — the NOT equal sign.' Write 5 + 3 ≠ 9 on the chart, the ≠ symbol highlighted (drawn as = with a slash through it).

More practice: 6+4 vs 10. Equal. 7+2 vs 8+2. Not equal (9 ≠ 10). 5-3 vs 1+1. Equal (both 2). Demonstrate each on the balance.

Now the rule. 'Bella says — the equal sign (=) means SAME AMOUNT. The NOT equal sign (≠) means DIFFERENT amounts.'

'Today we'll test lots of pairs to see which are equal and which aren't.'
student_actions: Watch Bella place counters on each pan.

steps.instruction: Whole group: test 4 more pairs on the balance. (a) 6+3 vs 5+4. Equal. (b) 8-2 vs 4+1. Not equal (6 ≠ 5). (c) 7+1 vs 9-1. Equal (both 8). (d) 10-3 vs 5+2. Equal (both 7).
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Four more pairs. Predict, then test.'

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 min each). Station A: Balance Drawings — pair has 8 cards; for each, draw counters on each pan of the balance drawing mat and write = or ≠. Station B: Equivalence Cards — pair has 16 expression-pair cards; sort into EQUAL and NOT EQUAL piles. Station C: Build Your Own — pair invents 4 pairs of expressions and tests each on a small balance.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each.'

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge at Station C: include 2 'looks-different but equal' cases (5+3 vs 7+1; 10-3 vs 4+3) and 2 'looks-similar but not equal' cases (4+4 vs 4+5; 8-2 vs 8-3). Discuss why looks can deceive.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to pairs: 'Some pairs LOOK obvious — but check carefully. Sometimes appearances trick you.'

steps.instruction: Discuss the equal sign. 'What does = mean?' Lead to: 'SAME AMOUNT.' NOT 'gives you the answer'. Distinguish: 5+3 = 8 means '5+3 is the same amount as 8'. 5+3 = 4+4 means '5+3 is the same amount as 4+4'.
steps.teacher_prompt: Use the balance scale to drive home the symmetry of the equal sign. The equal sign is BIDIRECTIONAL — both sides are the same.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the equivalence tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Hand them an expression pair and ask 'Equal or not? How do you know?' Mark the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Use only addition pairs (no subtraction yet). Limit to facts under 10.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch with 3-term expressions (1+2+3 vs 4+2). Discuss whether the rule extends.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide picture-supported expression cards. Sentence frame: '___ is equal/not equal to ___.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Allow them to be the 'balance' — physically tilt their arms based on which side is heavier.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: tests pairs correctly with the balance; uses = and ≠ symbols correctly; explains 'same amount' for the equal sign.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the equivalence tracker per child.

discussion_prompts: How does the balance scale show equal?
consolidation.exit_routine: Each child writes ONE pair they tested today on a sticky note: '___ ___ ___' (with = or ≠). Notes go on the chart on the way out.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Equivalence-testing accuracy, correct symbol use, and explanation of the equal sign meaning.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 2 captures C2.2 mastery. Children at L4 explain equal sign as 'same amount' (not 'gives the answer').

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child reads 5+3 = 4+4 as 'wrong because there's no answer' — repairing the operator misconception of the equal sign
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
The most common Grade-1 trap on C2.2 is the operator misconception: the child reads = as 'gives you the answer'. So 5+3 = 8 makes sense ('5+3 gives you 8'), but 5+3 = 4+4 doesn't ('5+3 doesn't give you 4+4'). They reject equations of the form expression = expression because they don't see how the right side is 'an answer'.

The distinction matters because the equal sign is BIDIRECTIONAL — both sides have the same value. A child who reads = as 'gives' will struggle with all algebraic thinking. The walkthrough covers the precise moment when a child rejects 5+3 = 4+4 because 'there's no answer'.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station A. The card is '5+3 vs 4+4'. The child says 'They're not equal because there's no answer.' Or writes 5+3 ≠ 4+4 incorrectly.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'Tell me how you decided.' The child says 'Equal sign means GIVES YOU THE ANSWER. 5+3 gives 8, but 4+4 isn't an answer.' Pause. 'OK — but the equal sign actually means SAME AMOUNT. Watch.'

Use the balance scale. Place 5+3 (8 counters) on one pan. Place 4+4 (8 counters) on the other. Balance is LEVEL. 'Both sides have 8 counters. Both pans are the SAME. So 5+3 = 4+4 — they're equal AMOUNTS, even though the EXPRESSIONS look different.'

Now rewrite the equal sign meaning. 'Equal means SAME AMOUNT. Not gives you the answer. 5+3 = 8 because they're the same amount. 5+3 = 4+4 because they're the same amount. 8 = 8 because they're the same amount.'

If the child STILL resists: emphasise the SYMMETRY. 'The equal sign works both ways. 5+3 = 4+4 is fine. 4+4 = 5+3 is fine. They're both saying SAME AMOUNT.'

Long-term recovery: include expression-on-both-sides equations daily in warm-ups. 5+3 = 4+4. 7+2 = 6+3. Children build the bidirectional reading.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Reads = as 'gives you the answer' — rejects expression = expression. Most common at start of Lesson 2.
(Mid) Accepts with prompts; doesn't yet auto-read = as 'same amount'.
(Strong) Reads 5+3 = 4+4 as 'both sides have the same amount'. Writes equations both ways.
(Stretched) Volunteers that = is symmetric: 'I can write it 4+4 = 5+3 too. Same thing.'
common_misconceptions: = means 'gives you'. (Operator misconception. Repair: balance scale shows symmetry.)
Right side of = must be a single number. (Children expect '8' on the right, not '4+4'. Repair: explicit expression = expression demonstration.)
Equations are unidirectional. (Repair: explicitly write both 5+3=4+4 AND 4+4=5+3. Both valid.)
recovery_moves: Always say 'same amount' aloud when reading an equation. Trains the bidirectional reading.
Use the balance scale for the first 2-3 expression-on-both-sides equations. Visual proof.
Include equation = equation cases in daily warm-ups. Build the reflex.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of C2.2 (testing equivalence of expression pairs).

parts_outline.task: Six expression pairs. Child writes = or ≠ between them.
Four balance scale drawings. Each shows expressions on each pan; child draws the balance level (level or tipped) and writes = or ≠.
Open prompt: 'Write your own pair of expressions that are EQUAL. Write your own pair that are NOT EQUAL.'

expected_image_assets: Four blank balance scale drawings for Part 2
